source.text: בְּ/רֹ֣ב רְכֻלָּתְ/ךָ֗ מָל֧וּ תוֹכְ/ךָ֛ חָמָ֖ס וַֽ/תֶּחֱטָ֑א וָ/אֶחַלֶּלְ/ךָ֩ מֵ/הַ֨ר אֱלֹהִ֤ים וָֽ/אַבֶּדְ/ךָ֙ כְּר֣וּב הַ/סֹּכֵ֔ךְ מִ/תּ֖וֹךְ אַבְנֵי אֵֽשׁ־׃

translation.text: By the abundance of your trade[a], your midst was filled with violence, and you sinned; so I cast you as profane[b] from the mountain of God, and I destroyed you[c], O guardian cherub[d], from the midst of the stones of fire.

footnotes.text: Or 'your trading' or 'your commerce'; the Hebrew term can also carry the sense of 'trafficking.'
Or 'I cast you out as defiled.' The Hebrew verb means 'to profane' or 'treat as unholy,' likely with the sense of expulsion from a sacred place.

The selected Greek text has 'you were wounded' and 'the cherub brought you out' here (compare verse14). This makes the cherub the agent rather than the one addressed. It is an alternative versional form, not simply another rendering of unchanged pointed Hebrew; original priority is uncertain.
Or 'covering cherub.' The Hebrew participle literally means 'covering/overshadowing,' here rendered 'guardian' to express its protective sense.

lexical_decisions.rationale: ב + רֹב is a causal/instrumental expression here, introducing the means or circumstance by which the following corruption occurred. 'By the abundance of' preserves the Hebrew structure while remaining natural English.

The noun can denote trade, commerce, or trafficking. 'Your trade' is concise and idiomatic. 'Trafficking' can suggest illicit trade in English, which may over-specify the Hebrew, though the context is morally negative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: your midst was filled with violence
alternatives: they filled your midst with violence
your interior was filled with violence
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although מָל֧וּ is morphologically 3cp ('they filled'), the clause is idiomatically rendered as a passive/resultative in English: 'your midst was filled with violence.' This best reflects the Hebrew sense without forcing an unspecified subject. תוֹךְ is 'midst' or 'inner part'; 'your midst' preserves the metaphorical interior/social center.
חָמָס commonly denotes violence, often including ruthless wrongdoing. 'Violence' is the standard and most direct rendering here.
A straightforward rendering of the waw-consecutive verb. The simple coordination preserves the Hebrew flow; the causal nuance is carried by the larger sentence context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so I cast you as profane
alternatives: therefore I cast you out as defiled
therefore I expelled you as unclean
lexical_decisions.lexicon: WLC/OSHB source analysis; bounded passage comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: Pointed Piel wayyiqtol first-person action: I profaned you. The following from God's mountain supports contextual expulsion; cast you as profane is the retained English interpretation, not the verb's bare gloss. The selected Greek instead has passive you were wounded; do not treat that as the same verbal wording.
A literal rendering preserves the elevated, mythic-cultic imagery of the passage. 'Mountain of God' is a recognizable biblical expression.

lexical_decisions.lexicon: WLC/OSHB source analysis; bounded published Greek comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: The fixed WLC pointing is Piel wayyiqtol first person with second-person object: I destroyed you, followed by cherub address. A cherub-subject analysis requires an explicit alternative verb interpretation/form. The selected Greek has the cherub led/brought you, not merely a different English synonym with an unchanged Hebrew subject. Historical priority remains unresolved.
Standard English biblical rendering for כְּרוּב. Singular is required by the Hebrew.

lexical_decisions.lexicon: WLC/OSHB source analysis; bounded passage comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: The definite active participle modifies cherub and describes covering/overshadowing, expressed functionally as guardian. This verse has no mimshach adjective; anointed covering is not an alternative rendering of this word. The literal covering sense is disclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the midst of the stones of fire
alternatives: from among the stones of fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: A largely formal rendering preserves the enigmatic imagery. 'From the midst of' echoes the Hebrew מִתּוֹךְ closely; 'from among' is smoother but slightly less formal.

theological_decisions.issue: Whether to render the addressee in a way that resolves the debated identity of the figure (human king, mythic cherub, or typological/supernatural referent)
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Preserve the text's direct address and cherubic imagery without resolving the broader interpretive debate.
alternative_readings: Translate in a way that flattens the imagery into purely royal metaphor
Translate in a way that explicitly identifies Satan or a primordial angelic fall
theological_decisions.rationale: Pointed WLC gives divine destruction and addresses the cherub; the selected Greek makes the cherub the agent bringing the addressee out. Retain the Hebrew-target form provisionally and disclose the connected alternative without deciding Satan, Adam or a primordial fall. This is not proof of original priority.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy §3: Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.

value.rationale: From חלל in the piel, the sense is to profane, defile, or treat as unholy. 'I profaned you' is formally close and preserves the cultic/theological force. Because English readers may hear 'profane' as merely verbal abuse, a footnote preserves the sense 'cast out as defiled'.
A literal rendering preserves the elevated, mythic-cultic imagery of the passage. 'Mountain of God' is a recognizable biblical expression.

אבד in the piel/hiphil domain can mean destroy, cause to perish, or remove. 'Destroyed' is the most direct lexical equivalent, though in context it may include expulsion; that nuance is not strong enough to replace the primary gloss.
Standard English biblical rendering for כְּרוּב. Singular is required by the Hebrew.

From סכך, 'to cover, screen, shelter.' In this context modifying cherub, 'guardian' communicates the protective/overshadowing role in natural English. 'Covering' is more literal but opaque in modern English. The traditional 'anointed cherub that covers' is not supported by this Hebrew form in this verse.
